concept.name: Jump across the creek
concept.definition: The Wyckoff metaphor for a sign of strength that decisively carries price above the resistance ('creek') of an accumulation trading range, signaling that demand has overcome the range's supply. It marks the transition from Phase D toward Phase E markup.
concept.intuition: The market finally leaps over the stream of sellers that capped every rally in the base.
concept.mechanics: After accumulation phases A-C, price advances through the range's resistance zone on widening spread and relatively high volume. The jump is conventionally confirmed by a subsequent 'back-up to the creek' — a low-volume pullback that holds above the former resistance, now acting as support.
relationships: Backup to the edge of the creek
concept.failure_modes: A jump that lacks volume or quickly falls back into the range is a failed breakout (potentially an upthrust if the range was actually distribution); confirmation via the back-up is essential.
concept.misconceptions: Crossing resistance by any amount is not automatically a jump; the Wyckoff reading requires the price-volume character of an SOS, not merely a marginal new high.
concept.example: After months between 90 and 102, a stock rallies through 103 on triple average volume; a quiet dip to 101 holds, and the analyst treats the move as a confirmed jump across the creek.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
